items.followUp: Write any two chemical properties of non-metals.

rubric.why: One mark is awarded for one correct chemical reaction or property of metals.
rubric.description: States one chemical property of metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any correctly described reaction, such as reaction with oxygen, water, acids, or halogens, with the correct product(s).

rubric.why: A second distinct chemical property is required for full credit.
rubric.description: States a second, distinct chemical property of metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for another correctly described reaction and its product(s); do not award twice for the same property.

modelAnswer: Metals react with oxygen to form metal oxides, which are generally basic.
Many metals react with dilute acids to form a salt and hydrogen gas.

items.followUp: Define malleability and ductility, giving one use of each property.

rubric.why: Malleability is the ability to be shaped by hammering without breaking.
rubric.description: Defines malleability.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that metals can be beaten or hammered into thin sheets.

rubric.why: Ductility is the ability to be drawn into wire.
rubric.description: Defines ductility.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that metals can be drawn into wires.

modelAnswer: Malleability is the ability of a metal to be hammered or rolled into thin sheets without breaking.
Ductility is the ability of a metal to be drawn into wires.

items.followUp: Why is the third ionization energy of magnesium higher than its second ionization energy?

rubric.why: After the first electron is removed, the second electron is removed from a positive ion, not a neutral atom.
rubric.description: Identifies the ion formed after the first ionization.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the second electron is removed from Mg⁺.

rubric.why: The remaining electrons experience a stronger attraction to the nucleus, so removing the next electron requires more energy.
rubric.description: Explains why the second ionization energy is greater.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining the increased attraction to the nucleus or that more energy is needed to remove an electron from the positive ion.

modelAnswer: The first ionization of magnesium forms Mg⁺ by removing one electron from a neutral Mg atom.
The second electron is removed from the positively charged Mg⁺ ion, where it is attracted more strongly to the nucleus; therefore, more energy is required.

items.followUp: Write any four characteristics of cathode rays.

rubric.why: Cathode rays travel in straight lines and can produce shadows of objects placed in their path.
rubric.description: States their straight-line travel or shadow-producing property.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either correct characteristic.

rubric.why: Cathode rays consist of negatively charged particles and are deflected toward the positive plate in an electric field.
rubric.description: States their negative charge or electric deflection.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the negative charge or correct direction of electric deflection.

rubric.why: Cathode rays produce fluorescence when they strike certain materials.
rubric.description: States that they cause fluorescence.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the fluorescent glow caused when cathode rays strike a suitable material.

rubric.why: Any one further characteristic completes the required set of five characteristics.
rubric.description: States one additional valid characteristic.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a further characteristic, such as deflection by a magnetic field, possession of mass and kinetic energy, or being independent of the gas in the tube.

modelAnswer: Cathode rays travel in straight lines and cast shadows when an object is placed in their path.
They carry a negative charge and are deflected toward the positive plate in an electric field.
They produce fluorescence when they strike certain substances, such as zinc sulphide.
They are deflected by a magnetic field.
They consist of particles that have mass and kinetic energy.

items.followUp: Classify molecules according to the number of atoms they contain and give an example of each type.

rubric.why: The four molecule types are classified by the number of atoms in each molecule.
rubric.description: Identifies the basis of classification.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the classification is based on the number of atoms in a molecule.

rubric.why: A monoatomic molecule contains one atom; a correct example is required.
rubric.description: Gives a monoatomic molecule and example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct type-example pair.

rubric.why: A diatomic molecule contains two atoms; a correct example is required.
rubric.description: Gives a diatomic molecule and example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct type-example pair.

rubric.why: A triatomic molecule contains three atoms; a correct example is required.
rubric.description: Gives a triatomic molecule and example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct type-example pair.

rubric.why: A polyatomic molecule contains more than three atoms; a correct example is required.
rubric.description: Gives a polyatomic molecule and example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct type-example pair.

modelAnswer: Molecules are classified according to the number of atoms they contain.
A monoatomic molecule contains one atom; for example, He.
A diatomic molecule contains two atoms; for example, H₂.
A triatomic molecule contains three atoms; for example, H₂O.
A polyatomic molecule contains more than three atoms; for example, NH₃.

items.followUp: Explain how hydrogen bonding affects the boiling point and solubility of water.

rubric.why: Hydrogen bonding is an intermolecular attraction involving hydrogen bonded to a highly electronegative atom and a nearby electronegative atom.
rubric.description: Defines hydrogen bonding.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the intermolecular attraction between a hydrogen atom attached to a highly electronegative atom and a nearby electronegative atom.

rubric.why: Extra energy is needed to overcome the intermolecular hydrogen bonds, raising boiling points.
rubric.description: Explains the effect on boiling point.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that hydrogen bonding raises boiling point because more energy is required to separate the molecules.

rubric.why: Hydrogen bonding strengthens attraction between molecules and affects properties such as melting point, viscosity, and surface tension.
rubric.description: Gives another physical-property effect.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct effect on a physical property such as melting point, viscosity, or surface tension.

rubric.why: Substances able to hydrogen-bond with water tend to dissolve more readily in it.
rubric.description: Explains the effect on solubility.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking hydrogen bonding with increased solubility in water for substances capable of forming hydrogen bonds.

modelAnswer: Hydrogen bonding is the intermolecular attraction between a hydrogen atom bonded to a highly electronegative atom, such as oxygen, nitrogen, or fluorine, and a nearby electronegative atom.
Hydrogen bonds strengthen the attraction between molecules, so more energy is needed to separate them and the boiling point is higher.
Hydrogen bonding can also raise melting point, viscosity, and surface tension.
Substances that can form hydrogen bonds with water are generally more soluble in water.

items.followUp: In a salt solution, identify the solute and solvent and explain why.

rubric.why: The solute is the substance that dissolves in a solution.
rubric.description: Defines the solute.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the solute as the substance that is dissolved.

rubric.why: The solvent is the substance that dissolves the solute.
rubric.description: Defines the solvent.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the solvent as the substance that dissolves the solute.

rubric.why: The example must correctly identify the substance being dissolved.
rubric.description: Identifies the solute in the example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly naming sugar or salt as the solute in the chosen example.

rubric.why: The example must correctly identify the dissolving substance.
rubric.description: Identifies the solvent in the example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly naming water as the solvent in the example.

rubric.why: A clear example demonstrates the roles of solute and solvent in a solution.
rubric.description: Gives a suitable solution example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving a valid example such as sugar dissolved in water or salt dissolved in water.

modelAnswer: A solute is the substance that is dissolved in a solution.
A solvent is the substance that dissolves the solute.
For example, in sugar solution, sugar is the solute and water is the solvent.
The resulting homogeneous mixture is called a solution.

items.followUp: Define molecular formula and write the molecular and empirical formulae of glucose.

rubric.why: An empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.
rubric.description: Defines empirical formula.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it represents the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element.

rubric.why: Two correct examples of empirical formulae are required.
rubric.description: Gives two examples.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving two valid examples, such as H₂O and CH₂O (the empirical formula of glucose).

modelAnswer: An empirical formula shows the simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms of each element in a compound.
Examples are H₂O and CH₂O; CH₂O is the empirical formula of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆.
